name: Tradeoff Point
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: When One Lever Moves Two Dials in Opposite Directions: Tradeoff Points
lesson.summary: A tradeoff point is a decision that is a sensitivity point for more than one quality attribute at once, so improving one attribute necessarily degrades another, and no amount of clever engineering removes the choice.
lesson.body:
A tradeoff point is an architectural decision identified as a sensitivity point for two or more quality attributes, where the attributes move in opposing directions as the decision changes. A sensitivity point tells a review team that one dial is connected to a particular lever. A tradeoff point tells the team that the same lever is connected to a second dial, and turning it to improve the first dial turns the second dial the wrong way. Recognizing a tradeoff point is often the single most useful outcome of an ATAM evaluation, because it converts an argument that sounds like a technical disagreement into a decision the business actually has to own.

Block size in Bitcoin is the canonical blockchain example. Raise the block size limit and throughput improves, since more transactions fit in each block; this is the sensitivity point relationship for the performance scenario about confirming transactions during high demand. But the same increase raises the bandwidth, storage, and processing every full node needs to keep up with the chain, which pushes ordinary users toward running lighter, less independent software or trusting someone else's node entirely; this is the sensitivity point relationship for a decentralization or security scenario about how many independent parties can validate the chain themselves. Block size is a sensitivity point for both, moving throughput up and the practical ability to run a full node down. That is a tradeoff point, and it is the actual substance of the disagreement that produced the hard fork covered earlier: Bitcoin Cash's community weighted throughput more heavily, Bitcoin's community weighted the cost of running a node more heavily, and no architecture change resolves that disagreement because the tradeoff is structural, not a bug to be fixed.

Consensus finality time is another recurring tradeoff point. Shortening the time before a block is considered irreversible improves the user experience quality attribute, since payments settle faster, but it can weaken the security quality attribute, since less time has passed for the network to detect and reject a conflicting chain before users have already acted on the faster confirmation. Networks that boast near instant finality are making an explicit bet on this tradeoff, usually by concentrating more trust in a smaller, faster to coordinate validator set, which is itself a decentralization tradeoff layered on top of the first one.

The output an ATAM team records for a tradeoff point is not a recommendation to eliminate it, since structural tradeoffs generally cannot be eliminated by better engineering. The output is a clear statement of the tradeoff, expressed in the vocabulary of the utility tree's priorities, so the stakeholders who actually bear the consequences, not just the architects who wrote the code, can decide deliberately which side of the dial their business needs, rather than discovering the tradeoff only after a contentious fork has already split their community in two.
